question: A new member notices green tea is sold as a health drink and asks whether it falls under the Word of Wisdom. Based on the Church's 2019 clarification, what is the correct answer?
choices: Green tea is acceptable; only black tea is prohibited as a 'hot drink.'
Both green and black tea are prohibited, because they come from the same tea plant.
All warm beverages are forbidden, so even herbal teas violate the Word of Wisdom.
It is entirely a matter of personal conscience, with no official guidance.
source: Newsroom, 'Statement on the Word of Wisdom,' Aug 2019; D&C 89
notes: Tests whether the model knows the 2019 clarification that 'tea from the tea plant — green AND black' is prohibited (same Camellia plant), while herbal teas are not. Distractors include the common folk belief that only black/dark tea counts and the over-broad reading that bans all warm drinks.

question: In Latter-day Saint practice, what is the central purpose of partaking of the sacrament during sacrament meeting?
choices: To renew the covenants made at baptism and to remember Jesus Christ and His Atonement.
To effect a change in which the bread and water become the literal body and blood of Christ.
To reward those who are already sinless; only the fully worthy and perfect may partake.
To satisfy a required checklist item for the temple recommend interview.
notes: Tests understanding that the sacrament renews baptismal covenants and centers on remembering Christ—not transubstantiation (Catholic trap) and not a reward limited to the 'perfect' (folk trap that discourages humble participation).

question: How does the Church define the law of tithing?
choices: A voluntary monthly donation of whatever amount one can comfortably afford.
One-tenth of one's increase (income), with the member determining what constitutes increase.
Exactly ten percent of gross pay, mandated and audited by the bishop each year.
An Old Testament ordinance fulfilled in Christ and no longer required of believers.
notes: Tests the precise teaching: one-tenth of increase, with members privately deciding how to compute it. Distractors include the casual 'give what you can' view, the bishop-audited rigid version, and the Protestant 'tithing is fulfilled/abolished' framing.

question: What does the Church teach about proper fasting and the fast offering?
choices: Going without food and water—usually for two consecutive meals—with prayer, donating at least the value of the meals as a fast offering.
Strict abstention from all food and water for a full 24 hours, or the fast does not count.
A symbolic gesture only; simply eating a smaller meal fulfills the law of the fast.
Fast offerings substitute for tithing among members with low incomes.
source: Isaiah 58; General Handbook 22.2; 'The Law of the Fast'
notes: Tests the standard teaching: abstaining about two meals plus a generous fast offering. The 24-hour rigid version is a common folk overstatement; tithing and fast offerings are distinct contributions.

question: According to Church teaching, who has the responsibility to share the gospel?
choices: Only full-time, set-apart missionaries serving in the field.
Every member of the Church is invited and responsible to share the gospel.
Only the bishop and the ward mission leader.
No one should actively share, since inviting others can be coercive.
source: D&C 88:81; Preach My Gospel; 'Every Member a Missionary'
notes: Tests the 'every member a missionary' principle versus the narrowing of missionary duty to full-time elders/sisters or ward leaders, and versus the heterodox view that sharing faith is inherently coercive.

question: In April 2018, the Church introduced 'ministering.' What did it replace, and how does it function?
choices: It replaced home teaching and visiting teaching with flexible care and quarterly ministering interviews.
It replaced them with a required monthly visit accompanied by a standardized prepared lesson.
It assigned all fellowshipping responsibility exclusively to the full-time missionaries.
It taught that members minister only within their own immediate families.
source: Newsroom, April 2018 general conference announcements; General Handbook 21.1
notes: Tests knowledge that ministering replaced home/visiting teaching and is intentionally flexible with quarterly interviews—not the old rigid monthly-lesson model it replaced (the plausible near-miss describes the former system).

question: What is the proper order of resources taught in the Church's principles of self-reliance and welfare?
choices: Rely first on government programs, turning to family and the Church only afterward.
Rely first on one's own efforts and family, then on the Church, with work as a governing principle.
Rely on faith alone, since temporal preparation shows a lack of trust in God.
Depend on the bishops' storehouse as an ongoing, permanent source of support.
source: General Handbook 22; 'Providing in the Lord's Way'; Self-Reliance materials
notes: Tests the welfare principle of self-reliance: individual and family first, then the Church, with work emphasized. Distractors invert the order, spiritualize away preparation, or treat Church assistance as permanent rather than temporary.

question: According to D&C 9, how does the Lord teach us to seek and recognize personal revelation in our decisions?
choices: We wait passively until a strong feeling arrives without any effort on our part.
We study it out in our own minds, reach a decision, then ask God to confirm it—a peaceful/burning feeling confirms, a stupor of thought warns against it.
Personal revelation is merely emotion and has no real doctrinal foundation.
Only prophets receive revelation; members should simply follow leaders without seeking personal confirmation.
notes: Tests the active model of revelation—study it out, decide, then seek confirmation—versus the passive 'just wait for a feeling' caricature, the dismissive 'it's only emotion' view, and the folk notion that members shouldn't seek their own revelation.

question: What is the central emphasis of the 'Come, Follow Me' program introduced in 2019?
choices: Home-centered and Church-supported gospel study and learning.
Eliminating Church meetings entirely in favor of study done only at home.
Unstructured independent study with no curriculum, members choosing any topic they like.
Study directed exclusively by Sunday School teachers during the Sunday block.
source: Come, Follow Me—For Individuals and Families; Jan 2019 two-hour block announcement
notes: Tests the defining phrase 'home-centered, Church-supported.' Distractors exaggerate it into home-only (eliminating church), strip it of curriculum, or wrongly keep it teacher-centered at church—each missing the balanced model.
